subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: In the small-town lane behind the bus stand, Tanuja kept a torn notebook in her school bag. Every rupee she spent went in it: five for peanuts, ten for lemon soda, two for a pencil. At the end of the month she sat on the doorstep and added it up with her tongue between her teeth. "More than half is snacks!" Her cousin Farida peered over. "That's more than the bangles you wanted." The next week Tanuja carried guavas from the tree behind their house and skipped the corner shop. She finished saving for her paints two weeks early.

qa.q: What did most of Tanuja's money go on?
qa.a: More than half of it went on snacks.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she added up the snacks?
qa.a: Surprised, since she had not realised how much she spent on them.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do if she loses the notebook, and why?
qa.a: She could keep a running total on a calendar at home, so she can still see where the money goes.

qa.q: How does Farida see Tanuja's list?
qa.a: Farida is struck by how the small amounts add up to more than bangles, so the numbers make it real.

grounding: A girl writes down every rupee for a month, sees the snacks add up, swaps to fruit and reaches her goal early.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: On the first of March in Valencia, Valentina's grandmother gave her a small green notebook. "Write down every coin you spend, all month." Valentina did: 1.20 for a pastry at the bakery, 0.80 for gum, 1.50 for crisps after swimming. On the thirty-first she sat with her best friend Ines and added it all up in pencil. Snacks: eighteen euros. Everything else: four. She stared at the page. She was saving for roller skates and had been stuck at thirty euros for weeks. In April she packed an apple and a bag of almonds for swimming days, and the bakery became a Saturday thing. By mid-May the skates were in a box under her bed, three weeks sooner than she had guessed.

qa.q: How much had Valentina spent on snacks in March?
What does Valentina staring at the page suggest?
qa.a: She felt surprised, even a little shocked, that snacks had taken most of her money.

qa.q: What else could help Valentina keep the notebook useful?
qa.a: She could look over it with her grandmother each week rather than once a month, since spotting a pattern early lets her change sooner.

qa.q: How might Ines see the notebook plan?
qa.a: Ines helped add it up, so Ines saw the eighteen euros too and might be curious to try tracking spending as well.

grounding: A girl records every coin she spends for a month, sees how much goes on snacks and reaches her saving goal sooner by bringing food from home.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: Every Saturday at the Hillcrest hostel, the matron handed out tuck money from a locked box. For all of October, Trisha wrote each rupee in a thin notebook: 10 for chikki, 15 for juice, 20 for a samosa after football. On the last Sunday she added it up in the common room. Out of four hundred rupees, two hundred and sixty had gone on snacks. "That's more than half," said Varun, her twin, peering over. Trisha wanted a three-hundred-rupee torch for the class camping trip. In November she asked the mess in-charge if she could carry fruit from breakfast, and kept a banana or a guava in her kit bag for after football. By the third week of November, the torch money was ready.

qa.q: How much of the four hundred rupees went on snacks?
What might Trisha have felt when Varun said it was more than half?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a bit embarrassed, but it also seemed to make her determined to change.

qa.q: Which other approach could help Trisha if the fruit runs out?
qa.a: She could check the notebook every week instead of once a month, so she notices extra snack spending sooner.

qa.q: How does Varun see the notebook?
qa.a: Varun is curious and peers over; the plain total makes the pattern obvious even to someone else. 🤔

grounding: A hostel girl logs every rupee for a month, sees how much goes on snacks and switches to fruit to reach her saving goal.
